selection.method: highest remaining verified actor-primary profiles after Perry Como singer correction

profiles.name: Arthur Kohl
profiles.excerpt: Arthur Kohl was a durable New York radio repertory actor whose surviving work spans wartime drama, Quiet Please, Johnny Dollar and Theater Five.
profiles.bio_html:
Arthur Kohl worked in the New York radio repertory across several generations of network drama. His surviving credits place him in wartime literary programming, supernatural anthology, detective radio and the medium's later dramatic revivals.

Kohl appeared repeatedly on Quiet, Please and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, then continued into Theater Five during the 1960s. That span shows the kind of adaptable microphone career that did not depend on one continuing character.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Kohl, six Theater Five appearances, four Quiet, Please broadcasts, two Words at War episodes and one X Minus One performance.

profiles.name: Eddie Fields
profiles.excerpt: Eddie Fields was a flexible West Coast radio character actor whose credits range from private-eye drama and Night Beat to literary anthology and musical radio.
profiles.bio_html:
Eddie Fields belonged to the Hollywood radio repertory that moved constantly among detective stories, anthology drama, comedy and musical programs. His surviving cast record shows steady work across the late network-radio years rather than one signature part.

Fields appeared on Let George Do It, Night Beat, Broadway Is My Beat, Rocky Fortune and Screen Directors Playhouse, along with more formal productions such as NBC University Theater. The variety of those programs reflects a performer hired for range and reliability.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves four Let George Do It performances credited to Fields, three Night Beat appearances, two each on five additional series, and further work on Dr. Kildare.

profiles.name: G. Stanley Jones
profiles.excerpt: G. Stanley Jones built a long voice and screen career after radio, with twenty surviving Johnny Dollar performances forming the center of his GRH profile.
profiles.bio_html:
Gordon Stanley Jones was born in Toronto in 1926 and developed a career across radio, film, television and voice acting. His voice work often drew on strong character accents and sharply defined personalities.

Radio listeners heard Jones repeatedly on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, where his versatility fit the program's rotating gallery of clients, suspects and supporting characters. He later continued as a screen and voice actor, including narration and animation work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 20 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to G. Stanley Jones, making the detective series the strongest surviving concentration of his radio work in the archive.

profiles.name: Ilona Massey
profiles.excerpt: Ilona Massey combined operatic training, Hollywood glamour and radio espionage, starring as a secret agent in Top Secret while maintaining a substantial singing career.
profiles.bio_html:
Ilona Massey was born Ilona Hajmassy in Budapest in 1910 and trained as a singer before building an international career in film, stage, radio and nightclub performance. Hollywood promoted her as a glamorous European star, but music remained a real professional foundation throughout her career.

Radio gave Massey a continuing dramatic showcase in Top Secret, where she starred as an international agent moving through stories of espionage and wartime intrigue. Her accent and cultivated delivery, which had helped define her film persona, became central dramatic tools on the microphone.

Golden Radio Hour currently verifies six Top Secret performances credited to Massey and an appearance on The Railroad Hour. Her singing career is retained as a genuine second professional category alongside acting.

profiles.name: Laurette Fillbrandt
profiles.excerpt: Laurette Fillbrandt was a West Coast radio actress whose surviving credits are concentrated in The Whistler, Jeff Regan and Philip Marlowe.
profiles.bio_html:
Laurette Fillbrandt worked in the professional West Coast radio repertory during the years when mystery and private-eye drama were among the medium's busiest forms. Her broadcast record places her repeatedly in productions that relied on experienced supporting actors to create new characters every week.

She appeared most often in The Whistler, then moved through hard-boiled detective series including Jeff Regan, Investigator and The Adventures of Philip Marlowe. Those programs demanded natural dialogue and quick characterization rather than broad theatrical performance.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine The Whistler performances credited to Fillbrandt, six Jeff Regan, Investigator appearances, four The Adventures of Philip Marlowe broadcasts and one I Love a Mystery episode.

profiles.name: Martha Greenhouse
profiles.excerpt: Martha Greenhouse brought a respected New York stage career and decades of union leadership into the repertory of CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Martha Greenhouse was born in Omaha in 1921 and grew up in New York City, where she developed a long career on stage, film and television. She also became a prominent advocate for working actors through sustained service in performers' unions.

Greenhouse's theatre background made her a natural fit for CBS Radio Mystery Theater, whose New York repertory drew heavily on experienced stage actors. Across the series she moved among mystery, supernatural and contemporary dramatic roles without being tied to one recurring character.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 20 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Greenhouse, documenting the radio branch of a career that remained closely tied to New York performance.

profiles.name: Stan Watts
profiles.excerpt: Stan Watts was a recurring Theater Five actor whose twenty surviving GRH performances document the working repertory behind radio drama in the 1960s.
profiles.bio_html:
Stan Watts is best documented through Theater Five, ABC's weekday dramatic anthology of the mid-1960s. The series depended on a regular New York company capable of shifting rapidly among crime, science fiction, suspense and contemporary drama.

Watts returned repeatedly in that repertory rather than building his radio identity around one continuing character. That pattern is important in its own right: later network radio survived in part because dependable actors could establish a completely new role within a single half-hour broadcast.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 20 Theater Five performances credited to Watts, giving the archive a concentrated record of his work during one of network radio drama's final sustained daily runs.

profiles.name: Stefan Schnabel
profiles.excerpt: Stefan Schnabel fled Nazi Germany, joined Orson Welles and the Mercury Theatre, and built a radio career that eventually encompassed thousands of broadcasts.
profiles.bio_html:
Stefan Schnabel was born in Berlin in 1912, the son of pianist Artur Schnabel and contralto Therese Behr. After the Nazi rise to power forced the family from Germany, he worked with London's Old Vic and moved to the United States, where he joined Orson Welles's Mercury Theatre.

Schnabel became deeply involved in American radio, including the Mercury Theatre period and wartime broadcasting. Contemporary biographical accounts credit him with thousands of radio appearances across his career, alongside stage, film and later television work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves four The Shadow performances credited to Schnabel, three each on Cloak and Dagger, The Chase and Words at War, two each on Columbia Workshop and The Mercury Theatre on the Air, plus additional dramatic appearances.

profiles.name: Alexander Scourby
profiles.excerpt: Alexander Scourby transformed a distinguished radio acting voice into one of American narration's landmark careers, recording literature, documentaries and the Bible.
profiles.bio_html:
Alexander Scourby was born in Brooklyn in 1913 and trained as a stage actor before radio made his resonant voice widely known. Dramatic broadcasting in the 1940s sharpened the vocal control that later became the defining feature of his career.

Scourby went far beyond acting. He became one of the most celebrated narrators of the twentieth century, recording hundreds of Talking Books for blind readers, major works of literature and complete Bible recordings, while also narrating documentaries and hosting broadcasts. Narration and hosting therefore stand as a major second profession in his profile.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves seven CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Scourby, five X Minus One appearances, three Stroke of Fate episodes and additional work on CBS Radio Workshop, Columbia Workshop, Dimension X and Words at War.

profiles.name: Jane Webb
profiles.excerpt: Jane Webb grew from child entertainment into a substantial radio career before becoming a prolific animation voice actress in the 1960s and 1970s.
profiles.bio_html:
Jane Karyl Webb was born in 1925 and began performing professionally as a child. Radio became the first major arena of her acting career, with continuing work in serials and family programs before she moved into the broader dramatic repertory of the 1950s.

Webb's microphone career included The Bartons, Bachelor's Children, Dr. Kildare and later mystery and anthology drama. She eventually carried the same vocal versatility into animation, voicing characters including Batgirl, Catwoman, Betty Cooper and Veronica Lodge.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves three The Chase performances credited to Webb, two each on Barrie Craig, Broadway Is My Beat, Crime Classics and NBC University Theater, plus additional appearances across several dramatic series.
